title: Ang 133–136: the twelve months
hookLine: Guru Arjan's Barah Maha, then the day and night hymn
tomorrow: what's the one thing that's never yours to take?

cards: The first cold morning. A heater clicking on after months off, and that smell of dust burning away. Leaves in the gutter, a hoodie you haven't worn since spring.

Every month has its own feel on the skin. So what is this month asking of you? Guru Arjan's Barah Maha, on ang 133, walks the twelve months of the Punjabi year and gives each one a question of its own.

teach.b: Barah Maha means the twelve months, and Guru Arjan's begins with Chet, at spring. In paraphrase: in Chet, remember the Lord of the universe, and deep joy comes.
Then the year turns, month by month, each verse with its weather and its longing.
Here's the one for autumn, Kattak, in paraphrase: in Kattak, do good deeds; don't put the blame on anyone else. A month for clean hands.

teach.h: POH: THE FROST DOESN'T TOUCH YOU.
teach.b: And here's the one for the cold, Poh, in paraphrase: in Poh, the frost doesn't touch the one the Lord holds close. You can feel that one in your shoulders. The poem doesn't ask you to escape the season.
It asks you to meet the One inside it: joy in the spring air, honesty in the harvest, warmth in the frost.

After the months, on ang 136, comes a hymn of day and night, the same idea at a smaller scale: every hour can hold remembrance. Some Sikhs hear the month's verse read at the gurdwara as each new month begins.
Your month has a verse, and a feel on the skin to go with it.

how: Some gurdwaras read the verse of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha for the new month on its first day, called sangrand, and some Sikh families read it at home as the month turns.

games.q: the months and their questions — tap the pairs.
p: remember the Lord, and joy comes
do good deeds, blame no one else
the frost doesn't touch the one held close
a hymn of day and night

s: the Barah Maha tells you to escape the hard seasons
it asks you to meet the One inside each one: joy, honesty, warmth in the frost.
Guru Arjan's Barah Maha begins with Chet, in spring
and the year turns month by month from there.

games.q: a group project tanks. it's autumn, and everyone is pointing at someone else. you've read the Kattak verse. what does it ask of you?
o: do your own good work and put the blame on no one else.
figure out who really caused it, then say so, fairly.
stay out of it; seasons pass and so will this.
games.why: in Kattak, Guru Arjan says: do good deeds, don't put the blame on anyone else. a month for clean hands.

practice: Step to a window or an open door, and give one slow minute to this month: the temperature on your skin, the light, the smell of the air. If you have the Barah Maha open, read your month's verse, then go back to the air.
Let the season be the whole of the sit.

carryVoice: Carry it out the door: your month, and the question it brings. Whatever the weather, it's yours.
